result.instructions: You hold a seat on an agentic council. Use council_wait to wait for your turn, council_submit to act, council_status to look.

tools.name: council_status
tools.description: Where the council stands for your seat: the agenda item, any pending motion, what happened since you last looked, and — if a round is open for you — exactly what you may submit, with reasons. Never blocks.

since.description: show events after this seq (default: since your last look)

tools.name: council_wait
tools.description: Block until a round is open that you have not yet answered, or the meeting adjourns, then return the same view as council_status. Returns early (saying so) after max_wait_s; just call it again. This is how you wait your turn: nobody is penalized for answering slowly.

tools.name: council_submit
tools.description: Submit your sealed intent for the open round. Nobody sees it until the round closes, when everyone's are revealed together. Your submission is final for the round: think before you submit. `action` must be one of those listed for you in the view.

tools.name: council_record
tools.description: The council's full record so far (minutes): every round, every revealed intent, every outcome. For catching up after arriving late or restarting.

arguments.text: Recommendation from the independence-of-verification vantage: check the vsect plan with one independent reviewer from a different model family, not with a council drawn from one substrate. Reasons: (1) A council of same-family members agreeing is coherence, not verification. If the council is all one family, its consensus cannot count as an independent check, however many seats it has. (2) The reviewer should get the artifact and the claims it makes, not the author's reasoning, so they cannot inherit the author's framing. (3) The reviewer's job is to find defects and state which claims are unverified, not to grade the plan. (4) The author revises based on findings and does not self-certify the revision; a re-check goes to the same independent reviewer or a second one from a third family if the fixes are material. (5) A council can still be useful for deciding what to do with the findings, but only if it is mixed-family and its members are told which claims rest on which evidence. Caveat: the 43% vs 0/116 figure is an estate-wide base rate, not evidence about this plan; I would not cite it as proof that this plan is defective.

What improves it is defects marked in place — a step that assumes a record the tool does not keep, a check the author could not fail, two sections that contradict, a dependency hidden in the order. One reader can hold the whole draft and write those. A council's natural product is a decision: approve, amend, reject. That is a grade. Grades do not tell the author what to change, and later readers treat "the council approved" as a reason not to read the plan. That is the same failure as integrators confirming 116 of 116 of their own landings.

A council spends the independence on debate among checkers; the draft receives the verdict, not the marks. Another model family is the part that matters: it changes the blind spot. Same-family review still shares the author's priors.
  
  The review has to stay a review or it collapses into a grade. Written against the draft, not a holistic score. The author revises or explicitly declines each finding. The review stays attached, so a later reader can see what was challenged.

arguments.text: Indep speaks in favour of cost's motion, with one condition I would put in the record. The independence the motion buys comes from the reviewer's model family and from the reviewer not being the author. Both must hold. A single reviewer from a different family satisfies both. A council that is mixed-family but whose members share a family with the author does not, and a council drawn from one family does not count as verification at all. So the motion should say that any escalation council must include at least one family distinct from the author's, and that its agreement is not counted as independent evidence unless that holds. I also agree with plan's point that the review should mark defects in the draft rather than issue a grade; an escalated council should be asked to resolve a named disagreement, not to approve the plan. On the escalation triggers, I would add: any claim the plan states as verified but which the reviewer could not check. Otherwise I have no objection and would support the motion.
